passage.title: The Reading Corner
passage.text:
When Teacher Amy moved to the mountain school, the classroom had a blackboard, thirty chairs, and no books. The nearest library was two hours away by bus. Most of her students, already in high school, had never finished a whole book.

She started with a single box. Each month she set aside part of her salary and bought three or four used books from a stall in the city. She wrote to her old classmates, and some sent books too. In six months the box became a shelf; by the end of the year, the shelf became a corner with a mat, two pillows, and a hand-painted sign that said READ HERE.

The rule was simple: anyone could borrow a book for one week, and anyone who returned a book could borrow another. At first the students were careful, unwilling to touch the books, as if they might break. Then a boy named Dado read a book about volcanoes and could not stop talking about it. Soon students were arguing over who would get the next book about animals.

Teacher Amy noticed something else. Students who had struggled to read a paragraph were reading whole chapters. Their spelling improved without extra drills. "I did not teach them to read better," she said later. "I just gave them a reason to read."

words.meaning: tried hard to do something difficult
words.example: He struggled to lift the heavy box.
She was unwilling to leave the party early.
The coach made us do passing drills.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the text BEST supports the idea that books were hard to get at the mountain school?
choices: When Teacher Amy moved to the mountain school, the classroom had a blackboard, thirty chairs, and no books.
The nearest library was two hours away by bus.
She started with a single box.
The rule was simple.
items.why: A library two hours away by bus shows how hard it was to reach books. Having no books in the room says the class lacked them, but the distance proves they were hard to get.

items.prompt: How was the classroom at the END of the year different from the classroom at the START?
choices: It had fewer chairs.
It had a reading corner with books instead of no books at all.
It had a new blackboard.
It had moved to the city.
items.why: At the start the room had "no books." By the end of the year there was "a corner with a mat, two pillows, and a hand-painted sign."

items.prompt: Which sentence BEST supports the idea that Teacher Amy gave up something of her own to build the collection?
choices: She wrote to her old classmates, and some sent books too.
Each month she set aside part of her salary and bought three or four used books from a stall in the city.
In six months the box became a shelf.
Teacher Amy noticed something else.
items.why: Setting aside part of her salary every month is her own sacrifice. The books from classmates were not her money.

items.prompt: "The box became a shelf; the shelf became a corner." What does the author really mean?
choices: Teacher Amy built furniture out of the box.
The collection of books kept growing bigger.
The box was lost and replaced.
The students moved the books every month.
items.why: A box does not literally turn into a shelf. The sentence pictures the growing number of books: too many for a box, then too many for a shelf.

items.prompt: Anyone who returned a book could borrow another. What does the prefix re- mean in returned?
choices: Back or again
Not
Before
Without
items.why: re- means back or again. To return a book is to turn it back in, to bring it back.

items.prompt: At first the students were careful with the books. What does the suffix -ful tell you?
choices: Without care
Full of care
Caring again
One who cares
items.why: -ful means full of. Careful means full of care, which is why they were afraid to touch the books.

items.prompt: The students were unwilling to touch the books. What does unwilling mean?
choices: Not wanting to
Wanting to very much
Willing again
Able to
items.why: The prefix un- means not. Unwilling means not willing or not wanting to.

items.prompt: "As if they might break." What does this tell you about how the students treated the books?
choices: They threw them around.
They handled them very carefully, like fragile things.
They broke them on purpose.
They did not know what books were.
items.why: Treating books as if they were breakable means handling them with great care.

items.prompt: Dado "could not stop talking about" the volcano book. What does this expression mean?
choices: His mouth was stuck open.
He talked about the book all the time because he was so excited.
He was told to stop talking but refused.
He read the book out loud in class.
items.why: It is an exaggeration. Nobody literally cannot stop; it means he kept bringing the book up because it excited him, and that excitement spread to the others.

items.prompt: How did the students' attitude toward the books change after Dado read the volcano book?
choices: At first they fought over books; later they ignored them.
At first they were afraid to touch them; later they argued over who got the next one.
At first they read in the corner; later they read at home.
Their attitude did not change.
items.why: "At first the students were careful, unwilling to touch the books... Soon students were arguing over who would get the next book."

items.prompt: How were the students DIFFERENT at the end of the year compared to the start?
choices: They had fewer books.
They read whole chapters instead of struggling with a paragraph.
They stopped borrowing books.
They moved to the city.
items.why: "Students who had struggled to read a paragraph were reading whole chapters."

items.prompt: Which detail BEST supports the claim that reading improved the students' skills?
choices: The nearest library was two hours away.
The corner had a mat and two pillows.
Their spelling improved without extra drills.
Teacher Amy wrote to her classmates.
items.why: Improved spelling with no extra drills is direct evidence that reading itself made them better.
